_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: Why then is it taught “the male”: “then your valuation shall be: the male.” We derive it from the extra “the”: and not a tumtum.
tosafot:a1.1: In brief: Tosafot note that the exclusion comes from the extra word, not from “male” alone (Niddah 28b), and that this baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, as shown in Shabbat 136b, where Rav Ḥisda says Rabbi Yehuda did not call a hermaphrodite male in every respect, for then it would be valuated, and an unattributed Sifra is Rabbi Yehuda. They ask why Rabbi Yehuda needs an extra word to exclude a hermaphrodite from valuations, when he disqualifies it from sanctifying the water of the red heifer with no verse, and includes it in circumcision only from “every male.” They answer that by reasoning alone Rabbi Yehuda already places a hermaphrodite outside “male”: circumcision needs a verse to include it, and valuations need one so that we do not value it at least as a woman. Finally, in light of Yevamot 72b, where Rabbi Yehuda disqualifies it as “perhaps a woman,” they suggest that for him it is a doubt: circumcision includes it as a full male, and valuations exclude it as anomalous. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:a2.1: A man’s valuation and a woman’s are not equal, as explained in the section of Behar Sinai.
rashi:a2.2: “If a female”: we derive it from the extra “if”: and not a tumtum. The verse does not exclude it because of uncertainty, since before Heaven there is no uncertainty; it must be excluding it as a creature of its own kind.
rashi:a2.3: Omit the tumtum from here: the verse excludes only the hermaphrodite, as a creature of its own kind. A tumtum is valuated, and stringently, as a male.
gershom:a1.1: One might think it shall not be by a man’s valuation: since we do not impose the stricter amount out of doubt.
gershom:a2.1: But it shall be by a woman’s valuation, since hers is less than a man’s.
gershom:a3.1: Omit the tumtum from here: a tumtum is valuated out of uncertainty.
rashi:a3.1: “Whether male or female” is written of the peace offering. A verse does not exclude because of uncertainty; and besides, male and female are both fit for a peace offering. So it must be a creature of its own kind.
gershom:a4.1: “Whether male or female”: as written of the peace offering.
gershom:a5.1: Omit the tumtum from here, since it is sacred out of uncertainty.
rashi:a4.1: “A male, and not a female”: this is the one about the burnt offering I explained above, which excludes a tumtum. Since the verse excluded it, it is a creature of its own kind, as a verse does not exclude because of uncertainty. (In the next baraita we do not read “the one that copulated,” since that does not apply to birds.)
rashi:a4.2: To exclude a tumtum and a hermaphrodite: since a tumtum too is a creature of its own kind.
rashi:a5.1: That is worshipped: the whole baraita speaks of bird offerings.
rashi:a5.2: They render garments impure in the throat: like any carcass of a kosher bird, since its pinching is no valid pinching and it is a carcass. If it were not a creature of its own kind, why would its pinching be invalid? Either way: if it is male it is fit, and if female it is fit, since with birds the Torah made no distinction. And there is a further challenge from Rabbi Eliezer, who says “wherever you find male and female, you exclude a tumtum”: would a verse exclude an uncertainty? It must be a creature of its own kind; where the Torah excluded it, it is excluded, and with birds, where it did not, it is not.
tosafot:a6.1: A tumtum and a hermaphrodite do not render garments impure in the throat: the same applies to offering them, which is permitted, as the reason explains. But since the first tanna said “impure,” Rabbi Eliezer said “do not render impure.”
gershom:a6.1: That is worshipped as an idol, set aside for idol worship, a prostitute’s payment and the price of a dog: all these speak of turtledoves and young pigeons. If one pinched them, the sanctity of the altar does not take effect on them; they are carcasses and render garments impure in the throat. Evidently a tumtum is not sacred for the altar.
rashi:a9.1: They do not become consecrated by substitution: that is, even substitution, which takes effect on an animal with a permanent blemish, does not take effect on them. The reason is explained in tractate Temurah, chapter Yesh BaKorbanot (17a).
rashi:a9.2: And they do not render consecrated as substitutes: if they are sacred, they cannot make a substitute. How could they themselves be sacred? For example, if they were offspring of consecrated animals, sacred through their mothers. And if a tumtum is an uncertainty, why is it not sacred, either way?
gershom:a8.1: They do not become consecrated by substitution: if one wanted to make them substitutes for consecrated animals, they do not become sacred in their place. And if he consecrated them and wanted to exchange them for a non-sacred animal, they do not consecrate it; they are not strong enough for their substitute to take hold.
rashi:a10.1: An orphan: it resembles the others that are disqualified from birth. What is an orphan? As explained in Chullin, chapter two (38b): its mother died while giving birth to it; she departed toward death and it toward life.
gershom:a9.1: Remove the tumtum and insert the orphan: like the orphan whose mother, as she bore it, departed toward death while it departed toward life, and therefore it is not sacred, as we learn from “one who slaughters in place of its mother”: to exclude an orphan.
rashi:a11.1: Let us say it is a dispute of tanna’im: Rav Ḥisda’s view, since there is one who holds it is an uncertainty.
gershom:a10.1: Let us say it is a dispute of tanna’im: Rav Ḥisda’s statement. One view holds a tumtum is sacred out of uncertainty, and another holds that perhaps it is a creature of its own kind and not sacred.
tosafot:a12.1: And Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda comes to say, in the name of Rabbi Shimon, that a tumtum too is a creature of its own kind: this implies he holds a hermaphrodite is a creature of its own kind for the same reason. Even though the Gemara concludes that for him a tumtum that urinates from the female place is excluded as female, a hermaphrodite is still always a creature of its own kind. It is puzzling, since in Yevamot (81a) it appears that Rabbi Shimon considers it a definite male, according to Rabbi Yoḥanan there. One may answer that even if it were a definite male, he would exclude it by the word “male,” while a tumtum that urinates from the female place is excluded, by the conclusion here, as a definite female, since he is not concerned that the male organ was inverted.
rashi:b1.1: Everyone agrees a tumtum is not in doubt as a creature of its own kind: so you cannot make Rav Ḥisda a dispute of tanna’im by saying the tanna who holds it is a creature of its own kind follows the latter Rabbis. Rather, these tanna’im of the baraita disagree about this: all agree that if it urinates from the male place it is a male and sacred,
rashi:b1.2: and the first tanna holds we are concerned that perhaps its male organ was inverted: folded inside, so that it passes water where a female’s would be. Rabbi Shimon holds we do not say so; it is certainly a female. Rav Ḥisda’s “a tumtum, all agree, is an uncertainty” comes to teach that you should not say that for the latter Rabbis a tumtum too is a creature of its own kind and firstborn sanctity takes effect on no tumtum at all. Still, Rav Ḥisda holds there is a tanna who does not even consider it doubtful: urinating from the male place, it is male; from the female place, female. And all agree with Rav Ḥisda that sanctity does take effect on a tumtum.
tosafot:b2.1: When they disagree is where it urinates from the female place: so Rav Ḥisda’s “a tumtum, all agree, is an uncertainty” cannot refer to one that urinates from the male place, which is certainly male, but to one that urinates from the female place, and according to the first tanna; whereas Rabbi Shimon has no uncertainty about a tumtum at all. You might ask: how does Rav Ḥisda know that for the latter Rabbis it is sacred out of uncertainty; perhaps they hold like Rabbi Shimon and it is not sacred at all? One may answer that since they disagree about the hermaphrodite because it is a creature of its own kind, they cannot disagree about a tumtum, which for Rav Ḥisda no tanna considers a creature of its own kind; presumably they agree with the first tanna that it is sacred out of uncertainty, as Rabbi Yishmael does. And as for 57a, where Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda excludes a tumtum from animal tithe by comparison with offerings, though tithe draws no line between male and female: Rav Ḥisda says “omit the tumtum from here,” and so does Reish Lakish below.
gershom:b1.1: The doubt is whether it is male or female: we do not know whether, if it is torn open, it will be a definite male or a definite female.
gershom:b2.1: If it urinates from the male place, all agree it is a male, since in an animal the male place is far from the female place.
gershom:b3.1: When they disagree is where it urinates from the female place. One Sage, the first tanna, holds a tumtum is an uncertainty and sacred out of uncertainty, since we are concerned that perhaps its male organ was inverted into the female place, and it is a male with its blemish.
gershom:b4.1: And Rabbi Shimon [ben Yehuda] holds that wherever “male” is said, it excludes a tumtum and a hermaphrodite, since when it urinates from the female place it is certainly female.
rashi:b2.1: In accordance with that which Rabbi Ilai ruled: that is, Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda holds like this ruling. [Rashi’s text reads Rabbi Ilai where ours reads Rabbi Elazar.]
rashi:b2.2: Non-sacred: he says this of a firstborn, that it is not sacred, since it is certainly female. This Rabbi Ilai is an Amora, not the one in the baraita above who spoke in the name of Rabbi Yishmael.
gershom:b5.1: Like that which Rabbi Elazar (Rabbi Ilai) ruled: we are not concerned that perhaps its male organ was inverted toward its female organ; it is certainly female.
rashi:b3.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan wondered: about this ruling of Rabbi Ilai.
rashi:b3.2: Neither the first tanna nor Rabbi Yishmael of our mishna: they say a tumtum is slaughtered neither in the Temple nor in the country because it is an uncertainty; and Rabbi Yishmael disagrees only about the hermaphrodite, whose female organ counts as a crack.
gershom:b6.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan wondered: who is this who ruled so, without concern for the first tanna or for Rabbi Yishmael of our mishna? As we said, for the first tanna, granted, a tumtum may not be slaughtered in the country, since perhaps it is a male without a blemish; and Rabbi Yishmael holds it is a male with its blemish.
rashi:b4.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan does not hold like Rav Ḥisda: rather, the latter Rabbis say of a tumtum too that it is a creature of its own kind.
gershom:b7.1: He does not hold like Rav Ḥisda. [A later editor suggests reading: if he does not hold like Rav Ḥisda, let him say that he ruled, etc.] If so, he ruled like the Rabbis, who say it is not a firstborn and becomes non-sacred, to be shorn.
rashi:b4.2: If he does not hold so, why does he wonder? Rabbi Ilai ruled like the latter Rabbis.
rashi:b4.3: Leaves two, the first tanna and Rabbi Yishmael, and acts like one, the latter Rabbis.
gershom:b8.1: That is indeed what Rabbi Yoḥanan says in wondering about him: who leaves two, the first tanna and Rabbi Yishmael, and rules like one, the Rabbis?
rashi:b5.1: Since its male and female organs are in one place: they cannot be checked by urination. [But] in an animal there is no doubt at all, according to everyone. When the first tanna of our mishna says it is not slaughtered, he means one that urinates from the male place, which is certainly sacred: so it is not slaughtered in the country, and in the Temple too it is unfit, since it looks blemished, with no visible male organ, as we exclude it from offerings in several places: “the male, and not a tumtum.” Rabbi Yishmael speaks of the hermaphrodite, and the latter Rabbis too speak of the hermaphrodite; but about a tumtum all agree: urinating from the male place, male; from the female place, female. And Rabbi Ilai ruled according to all of them.
tosafot:b5.1: They said a tumtum is an uncertainty only in a person: he holds like Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda, and does not say this according to everyone, since for the first tanna of our mishna it is obviously an uncertainty, for he says it is slaughtered neither in the Temple nor in the country.
gershom:b9.1: And Rabbi Ilai, who ruled like Reish Lakish, also holds as Reish Lakish said: in one place, close to each other.
gershom:b10.1: Rav Oshaya objects, both to Rabbi Ilai and to Reish Lakish: let us be concerned, etc.
rashi:b6.1: Like Rabbi Meir? This is asked in surprise: do we take a lone opinion’s concern into account?
gershom:b11.1: Abaye said to him: like whom? You who said “let us be concerned” hold like Rabbi Meir, who alone is concerned for the minority, as with a minor boy and girl who do not perform ḥalitza. That is, the male organ’s being inverted to the female place is a minority case.
rashi:b7.1: You may even say the Rabbis: we can raise this challenge for them too, since it has changed in being a tumtum, it has changed, so that its male organ was inverted into its female place.
rashi:b7.2: And he answers: there are those who say it has changed. That is, there is a view that in an animal we say “since it has changed, it has changed”: the first tanna above, who disagrees with Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda and is concerned that it was inverted; and Rabbi Elazar holds like Rabbi Shimon.
gershom:b12.1: You may even say the Rabbis, who disagree with him on that point, agree here: since it has changed in being a tumtum, it has also changed, and we are concerned that perhaps its male organ was inverted into the female place.
gershom:b13.1: And there are those who say: although it has changed in being a tumtum, its male organ has not also changed into the female place.
rashi:b8.1: Let us say: whether we say “since it has changed” or not is a dispute of tanna’im.
rashi:b8.2: One who betrothed, his betrothal is a betrothal: stringently, and she needs a bill of divorce, since perhaps he is a male.
rashi:b8.3: Was betrothed, the betrothal is a betrothal: the man who betrothed the tumtum is forbidden to the tumtum’s relatives, such as its mother and sister, since perhaps it is a female.
gershom:b14.1: A tumtum who betrothed, the betrothal is a betrothal [a later editor adds: she is forbidden to the tumtum’s relatives and also needs a bill of divorce, as Rashi explains]: he is forbidden to her relatives; and if it was betrothed, the one who betrothed it is forbidden to its relatives. And it performs ḥalitza, since perhaps it is a male.
rashi:b9.1: And performs ḥalitza: stringently. If there is no brother but the tumtum, the sister-in-law needs its ḥalitza; but if there is another brother, the tumtum does not perform ḥalitza, since this tanna is also uncertain whether it is female.
rashi:b9.2: And they perform ḥalitza with its wife: a stringency, since perhaps it is a male.
rashi:b9.3: And enter into levirate marriage with its wife: either way. If it is a male, his brother properly performs levirate marriage; if it is a female, this brother simply marries a woman. But the tumtum itself does not perform levirate marriage, since it cannot father children, and “to establish a name for his brother” does not apply to it.
rashi:b9.4: Is it not that everyone holds like Rabbi Akiva, who said in Yevamot, chapter HaArel (79b): a eunuch from birth does not perform ḥalitza or levirate marriage, and his wife does not perform ḥalitza and is not taken in levirate marriage, since he never had a time of fitness.
gershom:b15.1: And it does not perform levirate marriage, as we learned in HaArel: her husband disqualifies her, since it is a promiscuous intercourse.
gershom:b16.1: And they perform ḥalitza with its wife and levirate marriage with its wife: either way. If she was his brother’s wife, he has fulfilled the mitzva of levirate marriage; if not, she was not forbidden to him.
rashi:b11.1: And this is what they disagree about: the one who says they take its wife in levirate marriage either way holds that if it is a male, his brother properly takes her, since we do not say “since it has changed in being a tumtum, it has also changed” so as to doubt whether it is a eunuch from birth, such that even if torn and found male it would be a eunuch, and a eunuch’s wife is not taken in levirate marriage.
rashi:b12.1: And the one who says she is not taken in levirate marriage holds we say “since it has changed” in being a tumtum, it has also changed, so that it may be a eunuch from birth even if found male. Therefore its wife is not taken in levirate marriage, lest they encounter a forbidden relation: as a male, its betrothal is valid, and as a eunuch from birth, its wife is not bound to the levir, so she is like a brother’s wife who has children, and one who takes her violates the prohibition of a brother’s wife. Still, she needs ḥalitza, since it is not certain that it is a eunuch.
gershom:b17.1: We do not say “since it has changed in being a tumtum, it has also changed in being a eunuch from birth.” It is not a eunuch from birth, and its wife needs ḥalitza or levirate marriage.
gershom:b18.1: And the one who says she performs ḥalitza and is not taken in levirate marriage holds we do say “since it has changed, it has changed,” to be a eunuch from birth. So she performs ḥalitza out of doubt, and is not taken in levirate marriage, since it is written “who will not build up his brother’s house,” and perhaps this is not his brother’s house.
rashi:b13.1: No, all say perhaps it has changed, and we are in doubt whether it is a eunuch from birth. The one who says she is taken in levirate marriage is Rabbi Eliezer, who says in chapter HaArel (Yevamot 80a): the wife of a eunuch from birth is taken in levirate marriage, since such people are healed in Alexandria of Egypt; so either way it is permitted. The one who says she is not follows Rabbi Akiva.
gershom:b19.1: The one that teaches “she performs ḥalitza and is taken in levirate marriage” is Rabbi Eliezer, who said in chapter HaArel: not so, a eunuch performs ḥalitza and they perform ḥalitza with his wife, since he can be cured.
gershom:b20.1: The one that teaches “she performs ḥalitza and is not taken in levirate marriage” is Rabbi Akiva, who said a eunuch from birth never had a time of fitness.
rashi:b14.1: And who is the tanna who holds like Rabbi Akiva and says she performs ḥalitza and is not taken in levirate marriage?
rashi:b14.2: He makes the tumtum a definite eunuch: then even ḥalitza should not be needed, since Rabbi Akiva does not require ḥalitza for the wife of a eunuch from birth.
gershom:b21.1: And who is the tanna following Rabbi Akiva? That is, which of Rabbi Akiva’s students stands behind “she performs ḥalitza and is not taken in levirate marriage”? It cannot be Rabbi Akiva himself, who said a eunuch from birth does not perform ḥalitza and they do not perform ḥalitza with his wife. If we say Rabbi Yehuda, his student, he certainly makes it a eunuch from birth, so why would she perform ḥalitza? As we learned: Rabbi Yehuda says, etc.
rashi:b16.1: Rather, Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda, who says “perhaps.” So she needs ḥalitza, since perhaps it is a male and perhaps not a eunuch; and she is not taken in levirate marriage, since perhaps it is a male and a eunuch, she is not bound to the levir, and he would encounter a brother’s wife who has children.
rashi:b16.2: Perhaps it will be torn, etc.: he speaks of a case where there are other brothers, that the tumtum should not perform ḥalitza, lest it be a eunuch from birth. But if there is no other, it performs ḥalitza, and its sister-in-law is not left without any release, since perhaps it is not a eunuch. Therefore its wife too needs ḥalitza, since perhaps it is not a eunuch, and she is not taken in levirate marriage, since perhaps it is.
gershom:b22.1: Rather, Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda, his student, as it is taught, etc. Since perhaps it will be found a eunuch from birth, but not certainly, she performs ḥalitza.
rashi:b17.1: Is that to say every tumtum that is torn open is found to be male, so that he is in doubt only about a eunuch from birth and not about a female?
rashi:b18.1: What is the difference between them: between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei, regarding a tumtum whose brother died, since both say it does not perform ḥalitza.
gershom:b23.1: [This note runs into Rava’s answer on 43a.] What is the difference between Rabbi Yehuda, who says it is certainly a eunuch from birth, and Rabbi Yosei, who says it is a doubt, when both say it does not perform ḥalitza? Rava said: whether it disqualifies her where there are brothers, and performs ḥalitza where there are none. For Rabbi Yosei [the text reads Rabbi Yehuda; the sense requires Rabbi Yosei], who says perhaps it will be found a eunuch from birth, it disqualifies her where there are brothers: if it made a levirate betrothal with her, we say perhaps it is not a eunuch, and it has disqualified her for the brothers; and if there are no brothers, it performs ḥalitza. For Rabbi Yehuda, who says it is like a eunuch, it neither disqualifies her where there are brothers nor performs ḥalitza where there are none. And when Rabbi Yosei says a tumtum does not perform ḥalitza, he means where there are brothers; where there are none, it does.
gershom:b24.1: The chapter is concluded. [It ends with Rava’s answer on 43a.]
